body.text: IN BRIEF
• On 7 October 2023, the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel left 1,200 people dead and 251 taken captive.
• Despite rising antisemitism, Australian Jewish figures say their communities continue to "live proudly and openly".
WARNING: This article contains distressing content.

Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom.

Hamas' 7 October 2023 attack was Israel's single deadliest day since the nation was founded in 1948. The militants rampaged through villages, a music festival and army bases, killing 1,200 people and dragging 251 hostages back to Gaza.

They included civilians, soldiers, men, women, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals. Most were freed in return for Palestinian prisoners during ceasefires between Israel and Hamas, but dozens did not survive.

"Freedom has completely changed the way I see life," said Emily Damari, 30, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza — a community roughly 5km east of Gaza — and released in January 2025.
Her ordeal taught her not to take anything for granted, she said.
"One day in captivity feels like one week. You want to give up at every moment, but I did not," said Damari, who has recently married and launched a clothing line in Israel.
"Today, I open the fridge and I say thank you. I drink cold water and I say thank you. I am thankful for everything, big things and little things. Gratitude has become central to who I am.
"Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again."

Eli Sharabi, 54, was seized from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri. His British-born wife Lianne and their two daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were slain by the attackers. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and killed in Gaza.
In February 2025, Sharabi was released, appearing emaciated and skeletally thin after 491 days of captivity, which he says included being held in a tunnel, hungry, shackled and beaten.

"I learned in captivity how precious every moment and every choice can be, and I carry that understanding with me now. I choose to look ahead, to keep going and to use the life I have in a meaningful way," said Sharabi.

Since his release, he has helped establish the Shalva Sharabi Family Centre with the disability charity Shalva, to treat families coping with trauma and disabilities — in commemoration of his own family lost.
"I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do."
His wife and daughters believed deeply in caring for others, he said.

"Their kindness and care for others will continue. Families will walk through these doors and receive help, care and hope in a place that carries their name. That gives me strength and makes me very proud."
'The daily struggle is immense'
Hagar Brodutch was seized from Kfar Aza with her three children and her neighbour's daughter, who fled to their house after her parents were killed. They were freed in a brief truce in November 2023.
Life after captivity, she said, can be far more complicated than the way it is sometimes portrayed.

"The daily struggle is immense, especially for children. I believe it will take many more years before captivity becomes just a shadow that walks alongside us, rather than something that defines who we are," said Brodutch.
Recently, Brodutch, 43, started taking pastry-baking classes, a passion she has long had.
"This is about much more than learning how to bake. It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future," she said.
"During my time in Hamas captivity, I began to understand that if I were released, returning to my previous life and working in management might no longer be possible.
"I chose pastry as a form of therapy, but also as a way to create something new for myself, with the hope that one day it could become my profession."
Kfar Aza was one of the hardest-hit communities in Hamas' attack.
Aviva Siegel, 65, was kidnapped with her husband Keith. She was released in November 2023, but Keith was held until February 2025.
Aviva joined the hostage release campaign movement in Israel while her husband was still being held.
Their reunion and her children and grandchildren, and even strangers she meets, give her strength every day, she says.
"I feel that I'm not alone and that there's so much love in this world and we need to keep it with both our hands," she said. "I feel very, very lucky to be alive."
Crowds mark October 7 anniversary at Bondi Beach
At home, hundreds of people have gathered at Bondi Beach to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
Following prayers at a service at the Bondi Pavilion, Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, remembered the moment he learned of the attack.
He said his brother-in-law told him: "Everything is changing ... we're in a war".
"Young Israelis went out to dance at the Nova Music Festival and never came home.
"Israelis who believed in peace ... they were all murdered just for being Jews and Israelis."
The attack has since taken on a more visceral and immediate fear after the carnage on Bondi Beach.

He said he believes there was a "direct line" between the attack on October 7 and the Bondi Beach attack — where 15 people were gunned down, including a 10-year-old girl and an elderly Holocaust survivor.
The massacre took place on the north side of Bondi Beach, during a celebration marking the first day of Hanukkah on 14 December 2025.
NSW Opposition leader Kelly Sloane said the "evil and hate of October 7" had come "closer to home".
"Our community has woken up again and again to graffiti, vandalism, firebombings," she said.
Sloane said she would "never leave the side" of the Jewish community and the community of Bondi following last year's attack.
"As terrible as it was, I am glad to be there ... with our Bondi community, our Jewish community."
Zionist Federation of Australia president Jeremy Leibler said the brutal violence in Israel had an immense impact on Australian Jews that was solidified after the Bondi massacre.

"October 7 is a day of mourning for the more than 1,200 innocent people murdered when Hamas-led terrorists invaded Israel, massacring families in their homes, hunting down young people at a music festival ... and dragging men, women, children and the elderly into Gaza as hostages," he said.

"Terror and antisemitism will not define Jewish life in Australia. We will continue to live proudly and openly as Jews, and nothing these groups do will weaken the bond between Australian Jewry, Australia and Israel."

Some pro-Palestinian supporters have drawn attention to the ensuing escalation of Israel's war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 people and wounded 175,000, according to the local health ministry.
One of the groups organising a vigil at Sydney's Town Hall is Jews against Occupation, representing dissident Jewish voices, with the event entitled "Don't let Israel steal the date."
It has been widely condemned as highly inflammatory and insensitive by political leaders, including NSW Premier Chris Minns.
